"Philosophy is to be studied, not for the sake of any definite answers...but rather for the sake of the questions themselves..."

While I understand that there's a place for philosophy, I don't agree with this sentiment. This line of logic can be applied to anything that doesn't result in an indefinite answer. Russell makes a point that this indefinite search renders the mind "great", yet by the very nature of his admittance, there is no evidence to support this. The only measurable result seems to be those who are philosophical have a deeper appreciation for philosophy, which is as relevant as those who enjoy collecting bottle caps have a deeper appreciation for bottle caps. With that said, I'd be interested to know what AskPhilosophy believes to be the most tangible benefit to philosophy aside from a deeper appreciation of imagination.

While I see what you're getting at, Russell also states, "these questions...diminish the dogmatic assurance which closes the mind against speculation..." Mere contemplation of philosophy remains inherently valuable by this alone. If, by entertaining ideas, we open our minds to a world of possibility, we then become more aware of perspectives outside our original dogmatic beliefs.

I think what Russell means when he says "great" is that one who contemplates philosophical questions cannot help but become greater in the realm of thought. For, to even think of such ideas enhances our reasoning capabilities along with our understanding of our place in the world.

So, you disagree for public policy reasons.

Here's the public policy. You cannot contract for things you do not own.

Patents are for a limited time. Once that time expires, you no longer hold the right to exclude someone from using it. Considering how complex today's products are and how dependent one patent is upon "prior art" and licensed development, to give someone a temporary exclusive license on the condition that they must continue to pay after your intellectual property right expires creates very large strings that could make it quite difficult to permit the full range of license-free post-patent uses to be implemented.

As for the Brulotte case, yes, this was specifically taken by the Supreme Court to decide whether to overturn it. Patent holder today went through a whole list of horrors that would happen if the law were not overturned. The court said that those things simply haven't happened in any significant way, and there was no good reason to upset the settled law.
